edges.description: Reproduces sclerostin resistance, but is more sensitive to DKK1 than the p.G171V allele, so it models the human substitution class rather than a single uniform escape mechanism.
edges.limitations: DKK1 sensitivity differs between the two HBM alleles, so this model does not support a claim that all first-beta-propeller substitutions escape both inhibitors equally. As with p.G171V it does not model the cranial morbidity.

nodes.description: Canonical Wnt/beta-catenin signalling in the osteoblast lineage runs above its normal set point. This is a qualitative change, not merely a quantitative one: the pathway is no longer under the control of the sclerostin feedback loop by which osteocytes normally restrain formation in response to mechanical and endocrine cues.

evidence.snippet: Other less common recessive or dominant sclerosing disorders, such as endosteal hyperostosis, sclerostosis, van Buchen disease and high bone mass syndrome, are due to mutations in two genes (LRP5 and SOST) of the Wnt pathway that induce increased osteoblast activity.

nodes.description: Progressive bony encroachment on the cranial foramina compresses the nerves passing through them. This is the main route by which an otherwise well-tolerated increase in bone mass becomes symptomatic disease, and it is the reason the neurological features are late and slowly progressive rather than congenital.

evidence.snippet: Neurological manifestations, previously considered absent in the disease, affect 19.4% of the patients.

nodes.description: Diffusely increased bone density, most pronounced at the cranial vault and the endosteal surfaces of the long bones. Unlike the resorption-failure osteopetroses the accumulated bone is architecturally competent, so it does not carry the fracture, marrow-failure and extramedullary-haematopoiesis consequences that follow from dense but brittle bone.

Formation predominantly thickens the endosteal surface and the cranial vault rather than expanding the metaphyses, which is why ADO1 lacks the Erlenmeyer flask deformity of the resorption-failure osteopetroses.

evidence.snippet: The identification of LRP5 gain-of-function mutations in autosomal dominant osteopetrosis type I prompted a revision of the classification scheme, and this form is now being included among the high-bone-mass diseases.

nodes.description: Heterozygous missense substitutions land in the amino-terminal first beta-propeller of LRP5, before the first EGF-like domain. The clustering is the mechanistic clue: this region is not the Wnt-binding or signal-transducing part of the receptor but the docking surface for the secreted inhibitors sclerostin and DKK1. Substitutions here therefore do not make the receptor intrinsically more active; they make it unavailable to the physiological brake.

nodes.description: The second HBM knock-in. It is worth listing separately from p.G171V because the two alleles behave differently under DKK1 challenge, which is evidence that the substitutions are not interchangeable even though both cause high bone mass.

The human HBM allele knocked into the mouse locus, so the receptor is expressed at endogenous level and dose. Its value is not that it makes bone dense but that it lets the escape-from-inhibition mechanism be tested directly: the mouse is challenged with overexpressed sclerostin and asked whether bone still responds.

Osteoclast numbers are low in vivo and the resorptive response to a stimulus is blunted, yet osteoclasts taken from the same patients behave normally in culture. Osteoclastogenesis, marker expression, morphology, localisation of ClC-7 and cathepsin K, and the ability to resorb bone are all preserved in vitro. The defect is therefore in the bone microenvironment, not in the osteoclast.
